stalagmite: A deposit more or less resembling an inverted stalactite, formed by calcareous water dropping on the floors of caverns; hence, a similar deposit of other material.
storehouse: 1. A building for keeping goods of any kind, especially provisions; a magazine; a repository; a warehouse. Joseph opened all the storehouses, and sold unto Egyptians. Gen. xli. 56. The Scripture of God is a storehouse abounding with estimable treasures of wisdom and knowledge. Hooker. 2. A mass or quality laid up. (old) Spenser.
stolid: Hopelessly insensible or stupid; not easily aroused or excited; dull; impassive; foolish.
staghorned: Having the mandibles large and palmate, or branched somewhat like the antlers of a stag; -- said of certain beetles.
store: 1. That which is accumulated, or massed together; a source from which supplies may be drawn; hence, an abundance; a great quantity, or a great number. The ships are fraught with store of victuals. | 1. To collect as a reserved supply; to accumulate; to lay away. Dora stored what little she could save. Tennyson. 2. To furnish; to supply; to replenish; esp., to stock or furnish against a future…
strockle: A shovel with a turned-up edge, for frit, sand, etc. [Written also strocal, strocle, strokal.]
stainer: 1. One who stains or tarnishes. 2. A workman who stains; as, a stainer of wood.
stranger: 1. One who is strange, foreign, or unknown. Specifically: -- (a) One who comes from a foreign land; a foreigner. I am a most poor woman and a stranger, Born out of your dominions. Shak. | To estrange; to alienate. (old) Shak.
sternwheel: Having a paddle wheel at the stern; as, a stern-wheel steamer.
stipulator: One who stipulates, contracts, or covenants.
stewartry: 1. An overseer or superintendent. "The stewartry of provisions." Tooke. 2. The office of a steward; stewardship. Byron. 3. In Scotland, the jurisdiction of a steward; also, the lands under such jurisdiction.
strook: imp. of Strike. Dryden. | A stroke. (old) Chaucer.
strigine: Of or pertaining to owls; owl-like.
standish: A stand, or case, for pen and ink. I bequeath to Dean Swift, Esq., my large silver standish. Swift.
straught: To stretch; to make straight. [Written also straucht.] [Scot.] Sir W. Scott.
stycerin: A triacid alcohol, related to glycerin, and obtained from certain styryl derivatives as a yellow, gummy, amorphous substance; - - called also phenyl glycerin.
streaminess: The state of being streamy; a trailing. R. A. Proctor.
staurolitic: Of or pertaining to staurolite; resembling or containing staurolite.
stirrup: 1. A kind of ring, or bent piece of metal, wood, leather, or the like, horizontal in one part for receiving the foot of a rider, and attached by a strap to the saddle, -- used to assist a person in mounting a horse, and to enable him to sit steadily in riding, as well as to relieve him by supporting a part of the weight of the body. Our host upon his stirpoes stood anon.
storminess: The state of being stormy; tempestuousness; biosteruousness; impetuousness.
stook: A small collection of sheaves set up in the field; a shock; in England, twelve sheaves. | To set up, as sheaves of grain, in stooks.
stabculture: A culture made by inoculating a solid medium, as gelatin, with the puncture of a needle or wire. The growths are usually of characteristic form.
sternson: The end of a ship's keelson, to which the sternpost is bolted; -- called also stern knee.
starosty: A castle and domain conferred on a nobleman for life. [Poland] Brande & C.
stilton: A peculiarly flavored unpressed cheese made from milk with cream added; -- so called from the village or parish of Stilton, England, where it was originally made. It is very rich in fat. Thus, in the outset he was gastronomic; discussed the dinner from the soup to the stilton. C. Lever.
strombite: A fossil shell of the genus Strombus.
stang: 1. A long bar; a pole; a shaft; a stake. 2. In land measure, a pole, rod, or perch. [Obs. or Prov. Eng.] Swift. Stang ball, a projectile consisting of two half balls united by a bar; a bar shot. | To shoot with pain. [Prov. Eng.]
stubbedness: The quality or state of being stubbed.
stinkweed: Stramonium. See Jamestown weed, and Datura.
stepper: One who, or that which, steps; as, a quick stepper.
starthroat: Any humming bird of the genus Heliomaster. The feathers of the throat have a brilliant metallic luster.
strain: 1. Race; stock; generation; descent; family. He is of a noble strain. Shak. stibonium: The hypothetical radical SbH4, analogous to ammonium; -- called also antimonium.
stercoranism: The doctrine or belief of the Stercoranists.
stratography: A description of an army, or of what belongs to an army.
statuette: A small statue; -- usually applied to a figure much less than life size, especially when of marble or bronze, or of plaster or clay as a preparation for the marble or bronze, as distinguished from a figure in terra cotta or the like. Cf. Figurine.
stablish: To settle permanently in a state; to make firm; to establish; to fix. (old) 2 Sam. vii. 13.
stratigraphic: Pertaining to, or depended upon, the order or arrangement of strata; as, stratigraphical evidence. -- Strat`i*graph"ic*al*ly, adv.
stagnant: 1. That stagnates; not flowing; not running in a current or steam; motionless; hence, impure or foul from want of motion; as, a stagnant lake or pond; stagnant blood in the veins. 2. stethoscopist: One skilled in the use of the stethoscope.
strategical: Of or pertaining to strategy; effected by artifice. -- Stra*te"gic*al*ly, adv. Strategic line (Mil.), a line joining strategic points. -- Strategic point (Mil.), any point or region in the theater or warlike operations which affords to its possessor an advantage over his opponent, as a mountain pass, a junction of rivers or roads, a fortress, etc.
stalkeyed: Having the eyes raised on a stalk, or peduncle; -- opposed to sessile-eyed. Said especially of podophthalmous crustaceans. Stalked- eyed crustaceans. (Zoöl.) See Podophthalmia.
standby: One who, or that which, stands by one in need; something upon which one relies for constant use or in an emergency.
stramineous: 1. Strawy; consisting of straw. Robinson. 2. Chaffy; like straw; straw-colored. Burton.
stout: 1. Strong; lusty; vigorous; robust; sinewy; muscular; hence, firm; resolute; dauntless. With hearts stern and stout. Chaucer. A stouter champion never handled sword. Shak. | A strong malt liquor; strong porter. Swift.
strictly: In a strict manner; closely; precisely.
stiffness: The quality or state of being stiff; as, the stiffness of cloth or of paste; stiffness of manner; stiffness of character. The vices of old age have the stiffness of it too. South.
stoping: The act of excavating in the form of stopes.
strongwater: 1. An acid. (old) 2. Distilled or ardent spirits; intoxicating liquor.
strigose: Set with stiff, straight bristles; hispid; as, a strigose leaf.
stail: A handle, as of a mop; a stale. [Eng.]
standpipe: 1. (Engin.) A vertical pipe, open at the top, between a hydrant and a reservoir, to equalize the flow of water; also, a large vertical pipe, near a pumping engine, into which water is forced up, so as to give it sufficient head to rise to the required level at a distance. 2.
stare: 1. To look with fixed eyes wide open, as through fear, wonder, surprise, impudence, etc.; to fasten an earnest and prolonged gaze on some object. For ever upon the ground I see thee stare. Chaucer. | To look earnestly at; to gaze at. I will stare him out of his wits. Shak. To stare in the face, to be before the eyes, or to be undeniably evident. "The law . . .
station: 1. The act of standing; also, attitude or pose in standing; posture. A station like the herald, Mercury. Shak. stew: 1. A small pond or pool where fish are kept for the table; a vivarium. [Obs. or Prov. Eng.] Chaucer. Evelyn. 2. An artificial bed of oysters. staves: pl. of Staff. "Banners, scarves and staves." R. Browning. Also (stavz), pl. of Stave.
stubbed: 1. Reduced to a stub; short and thick, like something truncated; blunt; obtuse. 2. Abounding in stubs; stubby. A bit of stubbed ground, once a wood. R. Browning. 3. Not nice or delicate; hardy; rugged. "Stubbed, vulgar constitutions." Berkley.
statoblast: One of a peculiar kind of internal buds, or germs, produced in the interior of certain Bryozoa and sponges, especially in the fresh- water species; -- also called winter buds. stalagmitical: Having the form or structure of stalagmites. -- Stal`ag*mit"ic*al*ly, adv.
stereochromy: A style of painting on plastered walls or stone, in which the colors are rendered permanent by sprinklings of water, in which is mixed a proportion of soluble glass (a silicate of soda).
strangely: 1. As something foreign, or not one's own; in a manner adapted to something foreign and strange. (old) Shak. 2. In the manner of one who does not know another; distantly; reservedly; coldly. You all look strangely on me. Shak. I do in justice charge thee . . . stateswoman: A woman concerned in public affairs. A rare stateswoman; I admire her bearing. B. Jonson.
stuttering: The act of one who stutters; -- restricted by some physiologists to defective speech due to inability to form the proper sounds, the breathing being normal, as distinguished from stammering. | Apt to stutter; hesitating; stammering. -- Stut"ter*ing*ly, adv.
stirt: Started; leaped. They privily be stirt into a well. Chaucer.
strategic: Of or pertaining to strategy; effected by artifice. -- Stra*te"gic*al*ly, adv. Strategic line (Mil.), a line joining strategic points. -- Strategic point (Mil.), any point or region in the theater or warlike operations which affords to its possessor an advantage over his opponent, as a mountain pass, a junction of rivers or roads, a fortress, etc.
stannel: The kestrel; -- called also standgale, standgall, stanchel, stand hawk, stannel hawk, steingale, stonegall. [Written also staniel, stannyel, and stanyel.] With what wing the staniel checks at it. Shak.
steer: A young male of the ox kind; especially, a common ox; a castrated taurine male from two to four years old. See the Note under Ox. | To castrate; -- said of male calves.
stanchness: The quality or state of being stanch.
stackyard: A yard or inclosure for stacks of hay or grain. A. Smith.
stab: 1. To pierce with a pointed weapon; to wound or kill by the thrust of a pointed instrument; as, to stab a man with a dagger; also, to thrust; as, to stab a dagger into a person. 2. | 1. staving: A cassing or lining of staves; especially, one encircling a water wheel.
stoutly: In a stout manner; lustily; boldly; obstinately; as, he stoutly defended himself.
starspangled: Spangled or studded with stars. Star-spangled banner, the popular name for the national ensign of the United States. F. S. Key.
stufa: A jet of steam issuing from a fissure in the earth.
struthio: A genus of birds including the African ostriches.
statued: Adorned with statues. "The statued hall." Longfellow. "Statued niches." G. Eliot.
stylohyal: A segment in the hyoidean arch between the epihyal and tympanohyal.
stilpnomelane: A black or greenish black mineral occurring in foliated flates, also in velvety bronze-colored incrustations. It is a hydrous silicate of iron and alumina.
stirrer: One who, or that which, stirs something; also, one who moves about, especially after sleep; as, an early stirrer. Shak. Stirrer up, an instigator or inciter. Atterbury.
starchedness: The quality or state of being starched; stiffness in manners; formality.
sthenic: Strong; active; -- said especially of morbid states attended with excessive action of the heart and blood vessels, and characterized by strength and activity of the muscular and nervous system; as, a sthenic fever. Sthenic theory. See Stimulism (a).
startlish: Easily startled; apt to start; startish; skittish; -- said especially of a hourse. [Colloq.]
steadfastness: The quality or state of being steadfast; firmness; fixedness; constancy. "The steadfastness of your faith." Col. ii. 5. To prove her wifehood and her steadfastness. Chaucer.
structural: 1. Of or pertaining to structure; affecting structure; as, a structural error. 2. (Biol.) ster: A suffix denoting the agent (originally a woman), especially a person who does something with skill or as an occupation; as in spinster (originally, a woman who spins), songster, baxter (= bakester), youngster.
steedless: Having no steed; without a horse.
strabismus: An affection of one or both eyes, in which the optic axes can not be directed to the same object, -- a defect due either to undue contraction or to undue relaxation of one or more of the muscles which move the eyeball; squinting; cross-eye.
stillhouse: A house in which distillation is carried on; a distillery.
stereogram: A diagram or picture which represents objects in such a way as to give the impression of relief or solidity; also, a stereograph.
stagehouse: A house where a stage regularly stops for passengers or a relay of horses.
stramazoun: A direct descending blow with the edge of a sword. (old) B. Jonson.
stomatoscope: An apparatus for examining the interior of the mouth.
sticked: Stuck. And in the sand her ship sticked so fast. Chaucer. They sticked not to give their bodies to be burnt. Sir T. Browne.
stultiloquy: Foolish talk; silly discource; babbling. Jer. Taylor.
striate: To mark with striaæ. "Striated longitudinally." Owen. | Marked with striaæ, or fine grooves, or lines of color; showing narrow structural bands or lines; as, a striated crystal; striated muscular fiber.
stagedirector: One who prepares a play for production. He arranges the details of the stage settings, the business to be used, all stage effects, and instructs the actors, excepting usually the star, in the general interpretation of their parts.
stereoelectric: Of or pertaining to the generation of electricity by means of solid bodies alone; as, a stereoelectric current is one obtained by means of solids, without any liquid.
strouding: Material for strouds; a kind of coarse cloth used in trade with the North American Indians.
steeple: A spire; also, the tower and spire taken together; the whole of a structure if the roof is of spire form. See Spire. "A weathercock on a steeple." Shak. Rood steeple. strict: 1. Strained; drawn close; tight; as, a strict embrace; a strict ligature. Dryden. 2. Tense; not relaxed; as, a strict fiber. 3. stunning: 1. Overpowering consciousness; overpowering the senses; especially, overpowering the sense of hearing; confounding with noise. 2. Striking or overpowering with astonishment, especially on account of excellence; as, stunning poetry. [Slang] C. Kingsley. -- Stun"ning*ly, adv. [Slang]
street: Originally, a paved way or road; a public highway; now commonly, a thoroughfare in a city or village, bordered by dwellings or business houses. He removed [the body of] Amasa from the street unto the field. Coverdale. At home or through the high street passing. Milton.
staminate: (a) Furnished with stamens; producing stamens. (b) Having stamens, but lacking pistils.
stultify: 1. To make foolish; to make a fool of; as, to stultify one by imposition; to stultify one's self by silly reasoning or conduct. Burke. 2. To regard as a fool, or as foolish. The modern sciolist stultifies all understanding but his own, and that which he conceives like his own. Hazlitt. 3.
strappado: A military punishment formerly practiced, which consisted in drawing an offender to the top of a beam and letting him fall to the length of the rope, by which means a limb was often dislocated. Shak. | To punish or torture by the strappado. Milton.
steem: See 1st and 2nd Stem. (old) Chaucer. | To gleam. (old) His head bald, that shone as any glass, . . . [And] stemed as a furnace of a leed [caldron]. Chaucer.
stoor: To rise in clouds, as dust. [Prov. Eng.] | Strong; powerful; hardy; bold; audacious. [Obs. or Scot.] O stronge lady stoor, what doest thou Chaucer.

statism: The art of governing a state; statecraft; policy. (old) The enemies of God . . . call our religion statism. South.
stile: 1. A pin set on the face of a dial, to cast a shadow; a style. See Style. Moxon. 2. Mode of composition. See Style. (old) May I not write in such a stile as this Bunyan. | 1. stillage: A low stool to keep the goods from touching the floor. Knight.
stature: The natural height of an animal body; -- generally used of the human body. Foreign men of mighty stature came. Dryden.
stichwort: A kind of chickweed (Stellaria Holostea). [Written also stitchwort.]
strapwork: A kind of ornament consisting of a narrow fillet or band folded, crossed, and interlaced.
stemple: A crossbar of wood in a shaft, serving as a step.
stagirite: A native of, or resident in, Stagira, in ancient Macedonia; especially, Aristotle. [Written also Stagyrite.]
strengthful: Abounding in strength; full of strength; strong. -- Strength"ful*ness, n. Florence my friend, in court my faction Not meanly strengthful. Marston.
styrolene: An unsaturated hydrocarbon, C8H8, obtained by the distillation of storax, by the decomposition of cinnamic acid, and by the condensation of acetylene, as a fragrant, aromatic, mobile liquid; -- called also phenyl ethylene, vinyl benzene, styrol, styrene, and cinnamene.
stearic: Pertaining to, or obtained from, stearin or tallow; resembling tallow. stellate: 1. Resembling a star; pointed or radiated, like the emblem of a star. 2. (Bot.) Starlike; having similar parts radiating from a common center; as, stellate flowers.
struma: 1. (Med.) Scrofula. 2. (Bot.) A cushionlike swelling on any organ; especially, that at the base of the capsule in many mosses.
stola: A long garment, descending to the ankles, worn by Roman women. The stola was not allowed to be worn by courtesans, or by women who had been divorced from their husbands. Fairholt.
stercoranist: A nickname formerly given to those who held, or were alleged to hold, that the consecrated elements in the eucharist undergo the process of digestion in the body of the recipient.
stored: Collected or accumulated as a reserve supply; as, stored electricity. It is charged with stored virtue. Bagehot.
staffier: An attendant bearing a staff. (old) "Staffiers on foot." Hudibras.
steed: A horse, especially a spirited horse for state of war; -- used chiefly in poetry or stately prose. "A knight upon a steed." Chaucer. Mounted upon a hot and fiery steed. Shak.
stearone: The ketone of stearic acid, obtained as a white crystalline substance, (C17H35)2.CO, by the distillation of calcium stearate.
stupor: 1. Great diminution or suspension of sensibility; suppression of sense or feeling; lethargy. 2. Intellectual insensibility; moral stupidity; heedlessness or inattention to one's interests.
stylopodium: An expansion at the base of the style, as in umbelliferous plants.
stercorary: A place, properly secured from the weather, for containing dung.

struck: imp. & p. p. of Strike. Struck jury (Law), a special jury, composed of persons having special knowledge or qualifications, selected by striking from the panel of jurors a certain number for each party, leaving the number required by law to try the cause.
strepitores: A division of birds, including the clamatorial and picarian birds, which do not have well developed singing organs.

stagworm: The larve of any species of botfly which is parasitic upon the stag, as , which burrows beneath the skin, and Cephalomyia auribarbis, which lives in the nostrils.
strophic: Pertaining to, containing, or consisting of, strophes.
stemwinding: Wound by mechanism connected with the stem; as, a stem-winding watch.
stopover: Permitting one to stop over; as, a stop-over check or ticket. See To stop over, under Stop, v. i. [Railroad Cant, U.S.]
straightjoint: Having straight joints. Specifically: (a) Applied to a floor the boards of which are so laid that the joints form a continued line transverse to the length of the boards themselves. stroll: To wander on foot; to ramble idly or leisurely; to rove. These mothers stroll to beg sustenance for their helpless infants. Swift. Syn. -- To rove; roam; range; stray. | A wandering on foot; an idle and leisurely walk; a ramble.
student: 1. stoichiometric: Of or pertaining to stoichiometry; employed in, or obtained by, stoichiometry.
stephanion: The point on the side of the skull where the temporal line, or upper edge of the temporal fossa, crosses the coronal suture.

stateful: Full of state; stately. (old) "A stateful silence." Marston.

steppe: One of the vast plains in Southeastern Europe and in Asia, generally elevated, and free from wood, analogous to many of the prairies in Western North America. See Savanna. Steppe murrain. (Far.) See Rinderpest.
stem: To gleam. (old) His head bald, that shone as any glass, . . . [And] stemed as a furnace of a leed [caldron]. Chaucer. | A gleam of light; flame. (old)
story: A set of rooms on the same floor or level; a floor, or the space between two floors. Also, a horizontal division of a building's exterior considered architecturally, which need not correspond exactly… | 1. A narration or recital of that which has occurred; a description of past events; a history; a statement; a record. One malcontent who did indeed get a name in story. Barrow.
stegosauria: An extinct order of herbivorous dinosaurs, including the genera Stegosaurus, Omosaurus, and their allies.
stent: To keep within limits; to restain; to cause to stop, or cease; to stint. Then would he weep, he might not be stent. Chaucer. Yet n'ould she stent Her bitter railing and foul revilement. Spenser. | To stint; to stop; to cease. And of this cry they would never stenten. Chaucer.
sternway: The movement of a ship backward, or with her stern foremost.
stockholder: One who is a holder or proprietor of stock in the public funds, or in the funds of a bank or other stock company.
statistical: Of or pertaining to statistics; as, statistical knowledge, statistical tabulation.
starter: 1. One who, or that which, starts; as, a starter on a journey; the starter of a race. 2. A dog that rouses game.
steganopodous: Having all four toes webbed together.
stonebow: A kind of crossbow formerly used for shooting stones. Shak.
stunner: 1. One who, or that which, stuns. 2. Something striking or amazing in quality; something of extraordinary excellence. [Slang] Thackeray.
stall: 1. A stand; a station; a fixed spot; hence, the stand or place where a horse or an ox kept and fed; the division of a stable, or the compartment, for one horse, ox, or other animal. | 1. To put into a stall or stable; to keep in a stall or stalls; as, to stall an ox. Where King Latinus then his oxen stalled. Dryden. 2. To fatten; as, to stall cattle. [Prov. Eng.] 3.
stopped: Made by complete closure of the mouth organs; shut; -- said of certain consonants (p, b, t, d, etc.). H. Sweet.
starless: Being without stars; having no stars visible; as, a starless night. Milton.
statant: In a standing position; as, a lion statant.
stipitate: Supported by a stipe; elevated on a stipe, as the fronds of most ferns, or the pod of certain cruciferous plants.
stickit: Stuck; spoiled in making. [Scot.] Stickit minister, a candidate for the clerical office who fails, disqualified by incompetency or immorality.
stereochromic: Pertaining to the art of stereochromy; produced by stereochromy. -- Ste`re*o*chro"mic*al*ly, adv.
staw: To be fixed or set; to stay. [Prov. Eng.]
stibnite: A mineral of a lead-gray color and brilliant metallic luster, occurring in prismatic crystals; sulphide of antimony; -- called also antimony glance, and gray antimony.
stillborn: 1. Dead at the birth; as, a stillborn child. 2. Fig.: Abortive; as, a stillborn poem. Swift.
statistician: One versed in statistics; one who collects and classifies facts for statistics.
straggler: 1. One who straggles, or departs from the direct or proper course, or from the company to which he belongs; one who falls behind the rest; one who rambles without any settled direction. 2. A roving vagabond. Shak. 3. Something that shoots, or spreads out, beyond the rest, or too far; an exuberant growth. Let thy hand supply the pruning knife, And crop luxuriant stragglers.
stipe: (a) The stalk or petiole of a frond, as of a fern. (b) The stalk of a pistil. (c) The trunk of a tree. (d) The stem of a fungus or mushroom.
stemson: A piece of curved timber bolted to the stem, keelson, and apron in a ship's frame near the bow.
stocking: A close-fitting covering for the foot and leg, usually knit or woven. Blue stocking. See Bluestocking. -- Stocking frame, a machine for knitting stockings or other hosiery goods.
stiffening: 1. Act or process of making stiff. 2. Something used to make anything stiff. Stiffening order (Com.), a permission granted by the customs department to take cargo or ballast on board before the old cargo is out, in order to steady the ship.
start: 1. To leap; to jump. (old) 2. To move suddenly, as with a spring or leap, from surprise, pain, or other sudden feeling or emotion, or by a voluntary act. And maketh him out of his sleep to start. | 1. To cause to move suddenly; to disturb suddenly; to startle; to alarm; to rouse; to cause to flee or fly; as, the hounds started a fox. Upon malicious bravery dost thou come To start my quiet Shak.
stria: 1. A minute groove, or channel; a threadlike line, as of color; a narrow structural band or line; a striation; as, the striæ, or groovings, produced on a rock by a glacier passing over it; the striæ on the surface of a shell; a stria of nervous matter in the brain. 2. (Arch.) A fillet between the flutes of columns, pilasters, or the like. Oxf. Gloss.
stumptailed: Having a short, thick tail. Stump-tailed lizard (Zoöl.), a singular Australian scincoid lizard (Trachydosaurus rugosus) having a short, thick tail resembling its head in form; -- called also sleeping lizard.
standardbred: Bred in conformity to a standard. Specif., applied to a registered trotting horse which comes up to the standard adopted by the National Association of Trotting-horse Breeders. [U. S.]
stuck: imp. & p. p. of Stick. | A thrust. (old) Shak.
steerer: One who steers; as, a boat steerer.
stratify: To form or deposit in strata, or layers, as substances in the earth; to arrange in strata.
staggard: The male red deer when four years old.
stipule: An appendage at the base of petioles or leaves, usually somewhat resembling a small leaf in texture and appearance.
starriness: The quality or state of being starry; as, the starriness of the heavens.
sternutative: Having the quality of provoking to sneeze.
stoporder: An order that aims to limit losses by fixing a figure at which purchases shall be sold or sales bought in, as where stock is bought at 100 and the broker is directed to sell if the market price drops to 98.
stumper: 1. One who stumps. 2. A boastful person. [Slang] 3. A puzzling or incredible story. [Slang, U.S.]
steamship: A ship or seagoing vessel propelled by the power of steam; a steamer.
stover: Fodder for cattle, especially straw or coarse hay. Where live nibbling sheep, And flat meads thatched with stover them to keep. Shak. Thresh barley as yet but as need shall require, Fresh threshed for stover thy cattle desire. Tusser.
stably: In a stable manner; firmly; fixedly; steadily; as, a government stably settled.
streptothrix: A genus of bacilli occurring of the form of long, smooth and apparently branched threads, either straight or twisted.
steering: from Steer, v. Steering wheel (Naut.), the wheel by means of which the rudder of a vessel is turned and the vessel is steered.
sticky: Having the quality of sticking to a surface; adhesive; gluey; viscous; viscid; glutinous; tenacious. Herbs which last longest are those of strong smell, and with a sticky stalk. Bacon.
study: 1. A setting of the mind or thoughts upon a subject; hence, application of mind to books, arts, or science, or to any subject, for the purpose of acquiring knowledge. Hammond . . . | 1. To fix the mind closely upon a subject; to dwell upon anything in thought; to muse; to ponder. Chaucer. I found a moral first, and then studied for a fable. Swift. 2.
streamwheel: A wheel used for measuring, by its motion when submerged, the velocity of flowing water; a current wheel.
statuminate: To prop or support. (old) B. Jonson.
stroma: 1. (Anat.) (a) The connective tissue or supporting framework of an organ; as, the stroma of the kidney. (b) The spongy, colorless framework of a red blood corpuscle or other cell. 2. (Bot.) A layer or mass of cellular tissue, especially that part of the thallus of certain fungi which incloses the perithecia.
stabiliment: The act of making firm; firm support; establishment. Jer. taylor. They serve for stabiliment, propagation, and shade. Derham.
stearate: A salt of stearic acid; as, ordinary soap consists largely of sodium or potassium stearates.
sterlet: A small sturgeon (Acipenser ruthenus) found in the Caspian Sea and its rivers, and highly esteemed for its flavor. The finest caviare is made from its roe.
stupendous: Astonishing; wonderful; amazing; especially, astonishing in magnitude or elevation; as, a stupendous pile. "A stupendous sum." Macaulay. All are but parts of one stupendous whole. Pope. -- Stu*pen"dous*ly, adv. -- Stu*pen"dous*ness, n.
stalky: Hard as a stalk; resembling a stalk. At the top [it] bears a great stalky head. Mortimer.
stiddy: An anvil; also, a smith shop. See Stithy. [Prov. Eng.] Halliwell.
stingaree: Any sting ray. See under 6th Ray.
statical: 1. Resting; acting by mere weight without motion; as, statical pressure; static objects. 2. Pertaining to bodies at rest or in equilibrium. Statical electricity. See Note under Electricity, 1. -- Statical moment. See under Moment.
staphylomatous: Of or pertaining to staphyloma; affected with staphyloma.
stepfather: The husband of one's mother by a subsequent marriage.
stapelia: An extensive and curious genus of African plants of the natural order Asclepiadaceæ (Milkweed family). They are succulent plants without leaves, frequently covered with dark tubercles giving them a very grotesque appearance. The odor of the blossoms is like that of carrion.
steadfast: 1. Firmly fixed or established; fast fixed; firm. "This steadfast globe of earth." Spenser. 2. Not fickle or wavering; constant; firm; resolute; unswerving; steady. "Steadfast eye." Shak. Abide steadfast unto him [thy neighbor] in the time of his trouble. Ecclus. xxii. 23. Whom resist steadfast in the faith. 1 Pet. v. 9.
stickle: 1. To separate combatants by intervening. (old) When he [the angel] sees half of the Christians killed, and the rest in a fair way of being routed, he stickles betwixt the remainder of God's host and… | 1. To separate, as combatants; hence, to quiet, to appease, as disputants. (old) Which [question] violently they pursue, Nor stickled would they be. Drayton. 2. To intervene in;
stirte: imp. of Start, v. i. & t. Chaucer.
stationery: The articles usually sold by stationers, as paper, pens, ink, quills, blank books, etc. | Belonging to, or sold by, a stationer.
stripping: 1. The act of one who strips. The mutual bows and courtesies . . . are remants of the original prostrations and strippings of the captive. H. Spencer. Never were cows that required such stripping. Mrs. Gaskell. 2. pl. The last milk drawn from a cow at a milking.
structuralshape: The shape of a member especially adapted to structural purposes, esp. in giving the greatest strength with the least material. Hence, Colloq., any steel or iron member of such shape, as channel irons, I beams, T beams, etc., or, sometimes, a column, girder, etc., built up with such members.
strychnine: A very poisonous alkaloid resembling brucine, obtained from various species of plants, especially from species of Loganiaceæ, as from the seeds of the St. Ignatius bean (Strychnos Ignatia) and from nux vomica.
staphyline: Of or pertaining to the uvula or the palate.
styphnic: Pertaining to, or designating, a yellow crystalline astringent acid, (NO2)3.C6H.(OH)2, obtained by the action of nitric acid on resorcin. Styphnic acid resembles picric acid, but is not bitter. It acts like a strong dibasic acid, having a series of well defined salts.
straddling: Applied to spokes when they are arranged alternately in two circles in the hub. See Straddle, v. i., and Straddle, v. t., 3. Knight.
statuesquely: In a statuesque manner; in a way suggestive of a statue; like a statue. A character statuesquely simple in its details. Lowell.
stannous: Pertaining to, or containing, tin; specifically, designating those compounds in which the element has a lower valence as contrasted with stannic compounds. Stannous chloride (Chem.), a white crystalline substance, SnCl2.(H2O)2, obtained by dissolving tin in hydrochloric acid. It is used as a mordant in dyeing.
stull: A framework of timber covered with boards to support rubbish; also, a framework of boards to protect miners from falling stones. [Prov. Eng.]
stagecoach: A coach that runs regularly from one stage, station, or place to another, for the conveyance of passengers.
strabotomy: The operation for the removal of squinting by the division of such muscles as distort the eyeball.
strew: 1. To scatter; to spread by scattering; to cast or to throw loosely apart; -- used of solids, separated or separable into parts or particles; as, to strew seed in beds; to strew sand on or over a floor; to strew flowers over a grave. And strewed his mangled limbs about the field. Dryden. On a principal table a desk was open and many papers [were] strewn about. Beaconsfield. 2.
stagnate: 1. To cease to flow; to be motionless; as, blood stagnates in the veins of an animal; hence, to become impure or foul by want of motion; as, air stagnates in a close room. 2. | Stagnant. (old) "A stagnate mass of vapors." Young.
stationer: 1. A bookseller or publisher; -- formerly so called from his occupying a stand, or station, in the market place or elsewhere. (old) Dryden. 2. One who sells paper, pens, quills, inkstands, pencils, blank books, and other articles used in writing.
stampede: A wild, headlong scamper, or running away, of a number of animals; usually caused by fright; hence, any sudden flight or dispersion, as of a crowd or an army in consequence of a panic. | To run away in a panic; -- said droves of cattle, horses, etc., also of armies.
stern: Having a certain hardness or severity of nature, manner, or aspect; hard; severe; rigid; rigorous; austere; fixed; unchanging; unrelenting; hence, serious; resolute; harsh; as, a sternresolve; | 1. The helm or tiller of a vessel or boat; also, the rudder. (old) Chaucer. 2. (Naut.) The after or rear end of a ship or other vessel, or of a boat; the part opposite to the stem, or prow. 3.
stamineal: 1. Consisting of stamens or threads. 2. (Bot.) Of or pertaining to the stamens; possessing stamens; also, attached to the stamens; as, a stamineous nectary.
stated: 1. Settled; established; fixed. He is capable of corruption who receives more than what is the stated and unquestionable fee of his office. Addison. 2. Recurring at regular time; not occasional; as, stated preaching; stated business hours.
sterno: A combining form used in anatomy to indicate connection with, or relation to, the sternum; as, sternocostal, sternoscapular.
stanza: 1. A number of lines or verses forming a division of a song or poem, and agreeing in meter, rhyme, number of lines, etc., with other divisions; a part of a poem, ordinarily containing every variation of measure in that poem; a combination or arrangement of lines usually recurring; whether like or unlike, in measure.
stroker: One who strokes; also, one who pretends to cure by stroking. Cures worked by Greatrix the stroker. Bp. Warburton.
streptoneura: An extensive division of gastropod Mollusca in which the loop or visceral nerves is twisted, and the sexes separate. It is nearly to equivalent to Prosobranchiata.
stratum: 1. (Geol.) A bed of earth or rock of one kind, formed by natural causes, and consisting usually of a series of layers, which form a rock as it lies between beds of other kinds. Also used figuratively. 2. A bed or layer artificially made; a course.
stakeholder: The holder of a stake; one with whom the bets are deposited when a wager is laid.
stibine: Antimony hydride, or hydrogen antimonide, a colorless gas produced by the action of nascent hydrogen on antimony. It has a characteristic odor and burns with a characteristic greenish flame. Formerly called also antimoniureted hydrogen.
stinkpot: 1. An earthen jar charged with powder, grenades, and other materials of an offensive and suffocating smell, -- sometimes used in boarding an enemy's vessel. 2. A vessel in which disinfectants are burned. 3. (Zoöl.) The musk turtle, or musk tortoise. See under Musk.
stereotyped: 1. Formed into, or printed from, stereotype plates. 2. Fig.: Formed in a fixed, unchangeable manner; as, stereotyped opinions. Our civilization, with its stereotyped ways and smooth conventionalities. J. C. Shairp.
stereometer: 1. An instrument for measuring the solid contents of a body, or the capacity of a vessel; a volumenometer. 2. An instrument for determining the specific gravity of liquid bodies, porous bodies, and powders, as well as solids.
structurist: One who forms structures; a builder; a constructor.
storied: 1. Told in a story. 2. Having a history; interesting from the stories which pertain to it; venerable from the associations of the past. Some greedy minion, or imperious wife, The trophied arches, storied halls, invade. Pope. Can storied urn, or animated bust, Back to its mansion call the fleeting breath Gray. 3. Having (such or so many) stories; -- chiefly in composition;
stereoscope: An optical instrument for giving to pictures the appearance of solid forms, as seen in nature. It combines in one, through a bending of the rays of light, two pictures, taken for the purpose from points of view a little way apart. It is furnished with two eyeglasses, and by refraction or reflection the pictures are superimposed, so as to appear as one to the observer.
stylomastoid: Of or pertaining to the styloid and mastoid processes of the temporal bone.
stephanite: A sulphide of antimony and silver of an iron-black color and metallic luster; called also black silver, and brittle silver ore.
strid: A narrow passage between precipitous rocks or banks, which looks as if it might be crossed at a stride. [Prov. Eng.] Howitt. This striding place is called the Strid. Wordsworth.
streamlet: A small stream; a rivulet; a rill.
stay: A large, strong rope, employed to support a mast, by being extended from the head of one mast down to some other, or to some part of the vessel. Those which lead forward are called fore-and-aft… | 1. To stop from motion or falling; to prop; to fix firmly; to hold up; to support. Aaron and Hur stayed up his hands, the one on the one side, and the other on the other side. Ex. xvii. 12.
stormwind: A heavy wind; a wind that brings a storm; the blast of a storm. Longfellow.
startle: To move suddenly, or be excited, on feeling alarm; to start. Why shrinks the soul Back on herself, and startles at destruction Addison. | 1. To excite by sudden alarm, surprise, or apprehension; to frighten suddenly and not seriously; to alarm; to surprise. The supposition, at least, that angels do sometimes assume bodies need not…
stenograph: To write or report in stenographic characters. | A production of stenography; anything written in shorthand. I saw the reporters' room, in which they redact their hasty stenographs. Emerson.
stipulate: Furnished with stipules; as, a stipulate leaf. | To make an agreement or covenant with any person or company to do or forbear anything; to bargain; to contract; to settle terms; as, certain princes stipulated to assist each other in resisting the…
stumpage: 1. Timber in standing trees, -- often sold without the land at a fixed price per tree or per stump, the stumps being counted when the land is cleared. [Local, U.S.] Only trees above a certain size are allowed to be cut by loggers buying stumpage from the owners of land. C. S. Sargent. 2. A tax on the amount of timber cut, regulated by the price of lumber.
stenting: An opening in a wall in a coal mine. [Written also stenton.] [Prov. Eng.] Halliwell.
sterve: To die, or cause to die; to perish. See Starve. (old) Chaucer. Spenser.
stinkstone: One of the varieties of calcite, barite, and feldspar, which emit a fetid odor on being struck; -- called also swinestone.
styan: See Sty, a boil. De quincey.
stalled: Put or kept in a stall; hence, fatted. "A stalled ox." Prov. xv. 17.
stalactitic: Of or pertaining to a stalactite; having the form or characters of a stalactite; stalactic.
stahlism: The Stahlian theoru, that every vital action is function or operation of the soul.
stethal: One of the higher alcohols of the methane series, homologous with ethal, and found in small quantities as an ethereal salt of stearic acid in spermaceti.
strawberry: A fragrant edible berry, of a delicious taste and commonly of a red color, the fruit of a plant of the genus Fragaria, of which there are many varieties. Also, the plant bearing the fruit. The common American strawberry is Fragaria virginiana; the European, F. vesca. There are also other less common species. Strawberry bass. (Zoöl.) See Calico bass, under Calico.
styloid: 1. Styliform; as, the styloid process. 2. (Anat.) Of or pertaining to the styloid process. Styloid process (Anat.), a long and slender process from the lower side of the temporal bone of man, corresponding to the tympanohyal and stylohyal of other animals.
stricken: 1. Struck; smitten; wounded; as, the stricken deer. Note: [See Strike, n.] 2. Worn out; far gone; advanced. See Strike, v. t., 21. Abraham was old and well stricken in age. Gen. xxiv. 1. 3. Whole; entire; -- said of the hour as marked by the striking of a clock. [Scot.] He persevered for a stricken hour in such a torrent of unnecessary tattle. Sir W. Scott.
stormbeat: Beaten, injured, or impaired by storms. Spenser.
stringendo: Urging or hastening the time, as to a climax.
stromb: Any marine univalve mollusk of the genus Strombus and allied genera. See Conch, and Strombus.
starost: A nobleman who possessed a starosty. [Poland]
stepbrother: A brother by the marriage of one's father with the mother of another, or of one's mother with the father of another.
standel: A young tree, especially one reserved when others are cut. (old) Fuller.
strobiline: Of or pertaining to a strobile; strobilaceous; strobiliform; as, strobiline fruits.
statal: Of, pertaining to, or existing with reference to, a State of the American Union, as distinguished from the general government. I have no knowledge of any other kind of political citizenship, higher or lower, statal or national. Edward Bates.
strass: A brilliant glass, used in the manufacture of artificial paste gems, which consists essentially of a complex borosilicate of lead and potassium. Cf. Glass.
stockade: 1. (Mil.) A line of stout posts or timbers set firmly in the earth in contact with each other (and usually with loopholes) to form a barrier, or defensive fortification. [Written also stoccade.] 2. | To surround, fortify, or protect with a stockade.
staggerbush: An American shrub (Andromeda Mariana) having clusters of nodding white flowers. It grows in low, sandy places, and is said to poison lambs and calves. Gray.
stator: A stationary part in or about which another part (the rotor) revolves, esp. when both are large; as, (a) (Elec.) The stationary member of an electrical machine, as of an induction motor. (b) (Steam Turbine) The case inclosing a turbine wheel; the body of stationary blades or nozzles.
stereoscopy: The art or science of using the stereoscope, or of constructing the instrument or the views used with it.
statesgeneral: 1. In France, before the Revolution, the assembly of the three orders of the kingdom, namely, the clergy, the nobility, and the third estate, or commonalty. 2. In the Netherlands, the legislative body, composed of two chambers.
storkbilled: Having a bill like that of the stork.
stethoscope: An instrument used in auscultation for examining the organs of the chest, as the heart and lungs, by conveying to the ear of the examiner the sounds produced in the thorax. | To auscultate, or examine, with a stethoscope. M. W. Savage.
stoic: 1. A disciple of the philosopher Zeno; one of a Greek sect which held that men should be free from passion, unmoved by joy or grief, and should submit without complaint to unavoidable necessity, by… | 1. Of or pertaining to the Stoics; resembling the Stoics or their doctrines. 2. Not affected by passion; manifesting indifference to pleasure or pain. -- Sto"ic*al*ly, adv. -- Sto"ic*al*ness, n.
studio: The working room of an artist.
straighten: 1. To make straight; to reduce from a crooked to a straight form. 2. To make right or correct; to reduce to order; as, to straighten one's affairs; to straighten an account. | A variant of Straiten. [Obs. or R.]
staccato: 1. (Mus.) Disconnected; separated; distinct; -- a direction to perform the notes of a passage in a short, distinct, and pointed manner. It is opposed to legato, and often indicated by heavy accents written over or under the notes, or by dots when the performance is to be less distinct and emphatic. 2. Expressed in a brief, pointed manner.
straightener: One who, or that which, straightens.
strepsiptera: A group of small insects having the anterior wings rudimentary, and in the form of short and slender twisted appendages, while the posterior ones are large and membranous. They are parasitic in the larval state on bees, wasps, and the like; -- called also Rhipiptera. See Illust. under Rhipipter.
stereography: The art of delineating the forms of solid bodies on a plane; a branch of solid geometry which shows the construction of all solids which are regularly defined. Note: By cutting pieces of cardboard, or other suitable material, in the forms represented in the cut, folding them along the lines indicated, and joining their edges, the five regular solids may be formed.
stipulaceous: Of or pertaining to stipules; resembling stipules; furnished with stipules; growing on stipules, or close to them; occupying the position of stipules; as, stipular glands and stipular tendrils.
stalely: 1. In a state stale manner. 2. Of old; long since. (old) B. Jonson.
stratagemical: Containing stratagem; as, a stratagemical epistle. Swift.
stockdove: A common European wild pigeon (Columba ænas), so called because at one time believed to be the stock of the domestic pigeon, or, according to some, from its breeding in the stocks, or trunks, of trees. Note: The name is applied, also, to other related species, as the Indian stockdove (Palumbæna Eversmanni).
stimy: The position of two balls on the putting green such that, being more than six inches apart, one ball lies directly between the other and the hole at which the latter must be played; | To bring into the position of, or impede by, a stymie.
stimulus: 1. A goad; hence, something that rouses the mind or spirits; an incentive; as, the hope of gain is a powerful stimulus to labor and action. 2. That which excites or produces a temporary increase of vital action, either in the whole organism or in any of its parts;
steading: The brans, stables, cattle-yards, etc., of a farm; -- called also onstead, farmstead, farm offices, or farmery. [Prov. Eng. & Scot.]
strange: 1. Belonging to another country; foreign. "To seek strange strands." Chaucer. One of the strange queen's lords. Shak. I do not contemn the knowledge of strange and divers tongues. Ascham. 2. | Strangely. (old) Most strange, but yet most truly, will I speak. Shak.
streak: To stretch; to extend; hence, to lay out, as a dead body. [Obs. or Prov. Eng. & Scot.] | 1. A line or long mark of a different color from the ground; a stripe; a vein. What mean those colored streaks in heaven Milton. 2. (Shipbuilding) A strake. 3. (Min.) The fine powder or mark yielded…
sternal: Of or pertaining to the sternum; in the region of the sternum. Sternal ribs. See the Note under Rib, n., 1.
strangury: 1. (Med.) A painful discharge of urine, drop by drop, produced by spasmodic muscular contraction. 2. (Bot.) A swelling or other disease in a plant, occasioned by a ligature fastened tightly about it.
stasimon: In the Greek tragedy, a song of the chorus, continued without the interruption of dialogue or anapæstics. Liddell & Scott.
sterhydraulic: Pertaining to, or designating, a kind of hydraulic press; resembling such a press in action or principle. Sterhydraulic press, an hydraulic press producing pressure or motion by the introduction of a solid substance (as a long rod, or a cord wound on a roller) into a cylinder previously filled with a liquid.
strobilation: The act or phenomenon of spontaneously dividing transversely, as do certain species of annelids and helminths; transverse fission. See Illust. under Syllidian.
stiffneckedness: The quality or state of being stiff-necked; stubbornness.
stopple: That which stops or closes the mouth of a vessel; a stopper; as, a glass stopple; a cork stopple. | To close the mouth of anything with a stopple, or as with a stopple. Cowper.
stinter: One who, or that which, stints.
stayship: A remora, -- fabled to stop ships by attaching itself to them.
sterilizer: One that sterilizes anything; specif., an apparatus for sterilizing an organic fluid or mixture.
strontianite: Strontium carbonate, a mineral of a white, greenish, or yellowish color, usually occurring in fibrous massive forms, but sometimes in prismatic crystals.
strenger: , the original compar. & superl. of Strong. (old) Two of us shall strenger be than one. Chaucer.
stratigraphy: That branch of geology which treats of the arrangement and succession of strata.
starstereogram: A view of the universe of brighter stars as it would appear to an observer transported into space outside or beyond our universe of stars.
steamy: Consisting of, or resembling, steam; full of steam; vaporous; misty. Cowper.
stage: 1. A floor or story of a house. (old) Wyclif. 2. An elevated platform on which an orator may speak, a play be performed, an exhibition be presented, or the like. 3. | To exhibit upon a stage, or as upon a stage; to display publicly. Shak.
stronghand: Violence; force; power. It was their meaning to take what they needed by stronghand. Sir W. Raleigh.
stuffer: One who, or that which, stuffs.
stanchless: 1. Incapable of being stanched, or stopped. 2. Unquenchable; insatiable. (old) Shak.
stringpiece: (a) A long piece of timber, forming a margin or edge of any piece of construction; esp.: (b) One of the longitudinal pieces, supporting the treads and rises of a flight or run of stairs.
storge: Parental affection; the instinctive affection which animals have for their young.
styloglossal: Of or pertaining to styloid process and the tongue.
stellary: 1. Of or pertaining to stars; astral; as, a stellar figure; stellary orbs. [These soft fires] in part shed down Their stellar virtue. Milton. 2. Full of stars; starry; as, stellar regions.
stray: 1. To wander, as from a direct course; to deviate, or go out of the way. Thames among the wanton valleys strays. Denham. 2. To wander from company, or from the proper limits; to rove at large; | To cause to stray. (old) Shak.
stillroom: 1. A room for distilling. 2. An apartment in a house where liquors, preserves, and the like, are kept. [Eng.] Floors are rubbed bright, . . . stillroom and kitchen cleared for action. Dickens.
stride: 1. To walk with long steps, especially in a measured or pompous manner. Mars in the middle of the shining shield Is graved, and strides along the liquid field. Dryden. 2. | 1. To pass over at a step; to step over. "A debtor that not dares to stride a limit." Shak. 2. To straddle; to bestride. I mean to stride your steed. Shak.
streptobacteria: A so-called variety of bacterium, consisting in reality of several bacteria linked together in the form of a chain.
steadfastly: In a steadfast manner; firmly. Steadfast believe that whatever God has revealed is infallibly true. Wake.
steal: A handle; a stale, or stele. [Archaic or Prov. Eng.] And in his hand a huge poleax did bear. Whose steale was iron-studded but not long. Spenser. | 1. To take and carry away, feloniously; to take without right or leave, and with intent to keep wrongfully; as, to steal the personal goods of another. Maugre thy heed, thou must for indigence Or…
starcrossed: Not favored by the stars; ill-fated. (poetic) Shak. Such in my star-crossed destiny. Massinger.
stratified: Having its substance arranged in strata, or layers; as, stratified rock.
streamclock: An instrument for ascertaining the velocity of the blood in a vessel.
stowboard: A place into which rubbish is put. [Written also stowbord.]
stationary: 1. Not moving; not appearing to move; stable; fixed. Charles Wesley, who is a more stationary man, does not believe the story. Southey. 2. Not improving or getting worse; | One who, or that which, is stationary, as a planet when apparently it has neither progressive nor retrograde motion. Holland.
styx: The principal river of the lower world, which had to be crossed in passing to the regions of the dead.
stopship: A remora. It was fabled to stop ships by attaching itself to them. Sylvester.
statusquo: The state in which anything is already. The phrase is also used retrospectively, as when, on a treaty of place, matters return to the status quo ante bellum, or are left in statu quo ante bellum, i.e., the state (or, in the state) before the war.
sternebra: One of the segments of the sternum. -- Ster"ne*bral, a.
stayedness: 1. Staidness. (old) W. Whately. 2. Solidity; weight. Camden.
staminodium: An abortive stamen, or any organ modified from an abortive stamen.
stark: 1. Stiff; rigid. Chaucer. Whose senses all were straight benumbed and stark. Spenser. His heart gan wax as stark as marble stone. Spenser. Many a nobleman lies stark and stiff Under the hoofs of… | Wholly; entirely; absolutely; quite; as, stark mind. Shak. Held him strangled in his arms till he was stark dead. Fuller. Stark naked, wholly naked; quite bare. Strip your sword stark naked. Shak.
stream: 1. A current water or other fluid; a liquid flowing continuously in a line or course, either on the earth, as a river, brook, etc., or from a vessel, reservoir, or fountain; | 1. To issue or flow in a stream; to flow freely or in a current, as a fluid or whatever is likened to fluids; as, tears streamed from her eyes. Beneath those banks where rivers stream. Milton. 2.
storage: 1. The act of depositing in a store or warehouse for safe keeping; also, the safe keeping of goods in a warehouse. 2. Space for the safe keeping of goods. 3. The price changed for keeping goods in a store. Storage battery. (Physics) See the Note under Battery.
stelene: Resembling, or used as, a stela; columnar.
starkness: The quality or state of being stark.
stalker: 1. One who stalks. 2. A kind of fishing net.
stalkinghorse: 1. A horse, or a figure resembling a horse, behind which a hunter conceals himself from the game he is aiming to kill. 2. Fig.: Something used to cover up a secret project; a mask; a pretense. Hypocrisy is the devil's stalking-horse under an affectation of simplicity and religion. L'Estrange.
stabulation: 1. The act of stabling or housing beasts. 2. A place for lodging beasts; a stable. (old)
stomach: 1. (Anat.) An enlargement, or series of enlargements, in the anterior part of the alimentary canal, in which food is digested; any cavity in which digestion takes place in an animal; | 1. To resent; to remember with anger; to dislike. Shak. The lion began to show his teeth, and to stomach the affront. L'Estrange. The Parliament sit in that body . . .
stallage: 1. (Eng. Law) The right of erecting a stalls in fairs; rent paid for a stall. 2. Dung of cattle or horses, mixed with straw. (old)
stepstone: A stone laid before a door as a stair to rise on in entering the house.
struthious: Of or pertaining to the Struthiones, or Ostrich tribe.
stealthiness: The state, quality, or character of being stealthy; stealth.
standage: A reservior in which water accumulates at the bottom of a mine.
stonish: Stony. "Possessed with stonish insensibility." Robynson (More's Utopia).
stannoso: A combining form (also used adjectively) denoting relation to, or connection with, certain stannnous compounds.
stonechat: (a) A small, active, and very common European singing bird (Pratincola rubicola); -- called also chickstone, stonechacker, stonechatter, stoneclink, stonesmith. (b) The wheatear. (c) The blue titmouse. Note: The name is sometimes applied to various species of Saxicola, Pratincola, and allied genera; as, the pied stonechat of India (Saxicola picata).
standpoint: A fixed point or station; a basis or fundamental principle; a position from which objects or principles are viewed, and according to which they are compared and judged.
stomachical: 1. Of or pertaining to the stomach; as, stomachic vessels. 2. Strengthening to the stomach; exciting the action of the stomach; stomachal; cordial.
stallion: A male horse not castrated; a male horse kept for breeding.
stovain: A substance, C14H22O2NCl, the hydrochloride of an amino compound containing benzol, used, in solution with strychnine, as a local anæsthetic, esp. by injection into the sheath of the spinal cord, producing anæsthesia below the point of introduction.
stelography: The art of writing or inscribing characters on pillars. Stackhouse.
stot: 1. A horse. (old) Chaucer. Thorold Rogers. 2. A young bull or ox, especially one three years old. [Prov. Eng. & Scot.]
stonebird: The yellowlegs; -- called also stone snipe. See Tattler, 2. [Local, U.S.]
stithy: 1. An anvil. Sir W. Scott. 2. A smith's shop; a smithy; a smithery; a forge. "As foul as Vulcan's stithy." Shak. | To forge on an anvil. The forge that stithied Mars his helm. Shak.
steek: To pierce with a sharp instrument; hence, to stitch; to sew; also, to fix; to fasten. [Scot.]
stronghold: A fastness; a fort or fortress; fortfield place; a place of security.
stylagalmaic: Performing the office of columns; as, Atlantes and Caryatides are stylagalmaic figures or images. [Written also stylogalmaic.]
stablestand: The position of a man who is found at his standing in the forest, with a crossbow or a longbow bent, ready to shoot at a deer, or close by a tree with greyhounds in a leash ready to slip; -- one of the four presumptions that a man intends stealing the king's deer. Wharton.
stound: To be in pain or sorrow. [Obs. or Prov. Eng. & Scot.] | 1. A sudden, severe pain or grief; peril; alarm. (old) Spenser. 2. Astonishment; amazement. (old) Spenser. Gay.
structureless: Without a definite structure, or arrangement of parts; without organization; devoid of cells; homogeneous; as, a structureless membrane.
stamp: 1. To strike beat, or press forcibly with the bottom of the foot, or by thrusting the foot downward. Shak. He frets, he fumes, he stares, he stamps the ground. Dryden. 2. | 1. To strike; to beat; to crush. These cooks how they stamp and strain and grind. Chaucer. 2. To strike the foot forcibly downward. But starts, exclaims, and stamps, and raves, and dies. dennis.
stoneroot: A North American plant (Collinsonia Canadensis) having a very hard root; horse balm. See Horse balm, under Horse.
straightforward: Proceeding in a straight course or manner; not deviating; honest; frank. -- adv. In a straightforward manner. -- Straight`for"ward*ly, adv. -- Straight`for"ward*ness, n.
stupe: Cloth or flax dipped in warm water or medicaments and applied to a hurt or sore. | To foment with a stupe. Wiseman.
stress: 1. Distress. (old) Sad hersal of his heavy stress. Spenser. 2. Pressure, strain; -- used chiefly of immaterial things; except in mechanics; hence, urgency; importance; weight; significance. | 1. To press; to urge; to distress; to put to difficulties. Spenser. 2. To subject to stress, pressure, or strain.
styrax: 1. (Bot.) A genus of shrubs and trees, mostly American or Asiatic, abounding in resinous and aromatic substances. Styrax officinalis yields storax, and S. Benzoin yields benzoin. 2. Same as Storax.
stairhead: The head or top of a staircase.
stoutness: The state or quality of being stout. Syn. -- Strength; bulk; courage; force; valor; lustiness; brawniness; boldness; fortitude; stubbornness.
stagestruck: Fascinated by the stage; seized by a passionate desire to become an actor.
strong: 1. Having active physical power, or great physical power to act; having a power of exerting great bodily force; vigorous. That our oxen may be strong to labor. Ps. cxliv. 14. Orses the strong to greater strength must yield. Dryden. 2. Having passive physical power; having ability to bear or endure; firm; hale; sound; robust; as, a strong constitution; strong health. 3. Solid;
stevedore: One whose occupation is to load and unload vessels in port; one who stows a cargo in a hold.
stepson: A son of one's husband or wife by a former marriage.
steenkirk: A kind of neckcloth worn in a loose and disorderly fashion.
studious: 1. Given to study; devoted to the acquisition of knowledge from books; as, a studious scholar. 2. Given to thought, or to the examination of subjects by contemplation; contemplative. Locke. 3. Earnest in endeavors; aiming sedulously; attentive; observant; diligent; -- usually followed by an infinitive or by of; as, be studious to please;
studdingsail: A light sail set at the side of a principal or square sail of a vessel in free winds, to increase her speed. Its head is bent to a small spar which is called the studding-sail boom. See Illust. of Sail. Toten.
stageplayer: An actor on the stage; one whose occupation is to represent characters on the stage; as, Garrick was a celebrated stageplayer.
starlight: The light given by the stars. Nor walk by moon, Or glittering starlight, without thee is sweet. Milton. | Lighted by the stars, or by the stars only; as, a starlight night. A starlight evening and a morning fair. Dryden.
stringless: Having no strings. His tongue is now a stringless instrument. Shak.
stiver: A Dutch coin, and money of account, of the value of two cents, or about one penny sterling; hence, figuratively, anything of little worth.
stand: 1. To be at rest in an erect position; to be fixed in an upright or firm position; as: (a) To be supported on the feet, in an erect or nearly erect position; -- opposed to lie, sit, kneel, etc. | 1. To endure; to sustain; to bear; as, I can not stand the cold or the heat. 2. To resist, without yielding or receding; to withstand. "Love stood the siege." Dryden. He stood the furious foe. Pope.
stony: 1. Of or pertaining to stone, consisting of, or abounding in, stone or stones; resembling stone; hard; as, a stony tower; a stony cave; stony ground; a stony crust. 2. Converting into stone; petrifying; petrific. The stony dart of senseless cold. Spenser. 3. Inflexible; cruel; unrelenting; pitiless; obdurate; perverse; cold; morally hard; appearing as if petrified;
strapple: To hold or bind with, or as with, a strap; to entangle. (old) Chapman.
stelled: Firmly placed or fixed. (old) "The stelled fires" [the stars]. Shak. Note: [In this passage by some defined as "starry," as if from stellatus.]
stilar: Of or pertaining to the style of a dial. [Written also stylar.]
stentorophonic: Speaking or sounding very loud; stentorian. (old) Of this stentorophonic horn of Alexander there is a preserved in the Vatican. Derham.
straw: To spread or scatter. See Strew, and Strow. Chaucer. | 1. A stalk or stem of certain species of grain, pulse, etc., especially of wheat, rye, oats, barley, more rarely of buckwheat, beans, and pease. 2. The gathered and thrashed stalks of certain species…
staymaker: One whose occupation is to make stays.
steatite: A massive variety of talc, of a grayish green or brown color. It forms extensive beds, and is quarried for fireplaces and for coarse utensils. Called also potstone, lard stone, and soapstone.
strelitz: A soldier of the ancient Muscovite guard or Russian standing army; also, the guard itself.
strategus: The leader or commander of an army; a general.
stair: 1. One step of a series for ascending or descending to a different level; -- commonly applied to those within a building. 2. A series of steps, as for passing from one story of a house to another; -- commonly used in the plural; but originally used in the singular only. "I a winding stair found." Chaucer's Dream.
steersman: One who steers; the helmsman of a vessel. Milton.
stanchion: 1. (Arch.) A prop or support; a piece of timber in the form of a stake or post, used for a support or stay. 2. (Naut.) Any upright post or beam used as a support, as for the deck, the quarter rails, awnings, etc. 3. A vertical bar for confining cattle in a stall.
strickle: 1. An instrument to strike grain to a level with the measure; a strike. 2. An instrument for whetting scythes; a rifle. 3. (Founding) An instrument used for smoothing the surface of a core. 4. (Carp. & Mason.) A templet; a pattern. 5. An instrument used in dressing flax. [Prov. Eng.]
styracin: A white crystalline tasteless substance extracted from gum storax, and consisting of a salt of cinnamic acid with cinnamic alcohol.
stigmatic: 1. A notorious profligate or criminal who has been branded; one who bears the marks of infamy or punishment. Bullokar. 2. A person who is marked or deformed by nature. Shak. | 1. Marked with a stigma, or with something reproachful to character. 2. Impressing with infamy or reproach. 3. (Bot., Anat., etc) Of or pertaining to a stigma or stigmata.
streaming: 1. The act or operation of that which streams; the act of that which sends forth, or which runs in, streams. 2. (Mining) The reduction of stream tin; also, the search for stream tin.
stagemanager: One in control of the stage during the production of a play. He directs the stage hands, property man, etc., has charge of all details behind the curtain, except the acting, and has a general oversight of the actors. Sometimes he is also the stage director.
stonecrop: 1. A sort of tree. (old) Mortimer. 2. (Bot.) Any low succulent plant of the genus Sedum, esp. Sedum acre, which is common on bare rocks in Europe, and is spreading in parts of America. See Orpine. Virginian, or Ditch, stonecrop, an American plant (Penthorum sedoides).
stencil: A thin plate of metal, leather, or other material, used in painting, marking, etc. The pattern is cut out of the plate, which is then laid flat on the surface to be marked, and the color brushed over… | To mark, paint, or color in figures with stencils; to form or print by means of a stencil.
stomachal: 1. Of or pertaining to the stomach; gastric. 2. Helping the stomach; stomachic; cordial.
stereomonoscope: An instrument with two lenses, by which an image of a single picture projected upon a screen of ground glass is made to present an appearance of relief, and may be viewed by several persons at once.
studhorse: A stallion, esp. one kept for breeding.
stilbite: A common mineral of the zeolite family, a hydrous silicate of alumina and lime, usually occurring in sheaflike aggregations of crystals, also in radiated masses. It is of a white or yellowish color, with pearly luster on the cleavage surface. Called also desmine.
stretching: from Stretch, v. Stretching course (Masonry), a course or series of stretchers. See Stretcher, 2. Britton.
strategy: 1. The science of military command, or the science of projecting campaigns and directing great military movements; generalship. 2. The use of stratagem or artifice.
stratocumulus: Large balls or rolls of dark cloud which frequently cover the whole sky, esp. in winter, and give it at times an undulated appearance.
sterculiaceous: Of or pertaining to a natural order (Sterculiaceæ) of polypetalous exogenous plants, mostly tropical. The cacao (Theobroma Cacao) is the most useful plant of the order.
stillatory: 1. An alembic; a vessel for distillation. Bacon. 2. A laboratory; a place or room in which distillation is performed. Dr. H. More. Sir H. Wotton.
steve: To pack or stow, as cargo in a ship's hold. See Steeve.
stateliness: The quality or state of being stately. For stateliness and majesty, what is comparable to a horse Dr. H. More.
stylist: One who is a master or a model of style, especially in writing or speaking; a critic of style. Distinguished as a stylist, for ease. Fitzed. Hall.
stationariness: The quality or state of being stationary; fixity.
stenodermine: Of or pertaining to the genus Stenoderma, which includes several West Indian and South American nose-leaf bats.
stag: 1. (Zoöl.) (a) The adult male of the red deer (Cervus elaphus), a large European species closely related to the American elk, or wapiti. (b) The male of certain other species of large deer. 2. | To act as a "stag", or irregular dealer in stocks. [Cant]
strumstrum: A rude musical instrument somewhat like a cittern. Dampier.
statuesque: Partaking of, or exemplifying, the characteristics of a statue; having the symmetry, or other excellence, of a statue artistically made; as, statuesquelimbs; a statuesque attitude. Their characters are mostly statuesque even in this respect, that they have no background. Hare.
stith: Strong; stiff; rigid. [Obs. or Prov. Eng.] | An anvil; a stithy. [Obs. or Prov. Eng.] He invented also pincers, hammers, iron crows, and the anvil, or stith. Holland.
stippling: A mode of execution which produces the effect by dots or small points instead of lines. 2. (Paint.) A mode of execution in which a flat or even tint is produced by many small touches.
strangle: 1. To compress the windpipe of (a person or animal) until death results from stoppage of respiration; to choke to death by compressing the throat, as with the hand or a rope. | To be strangled, or suffocated.
stavesacre: A kind of larkspur (Delphinium Staphysagria), and its seeds, which are violently purgative and emetic. They are used as a parasiticide, and in the East for poisoning fish.
strull: A bar so placed as to resist weight.
staple: 1. A settled mart; an emporium; a city or town to which merchants brought commodities for sale or exportation in bulk; a place for wholesale traffic. The customs of Alexandria were very great, it… | 1. Pertaining to, or being market of staple for, commodities; as, a staple town. 2. Established in commerce; occupying the markets; settled; as, a staple trade. Dryden. 3. Fit to be sold; marketable.
stonestill: As still as a stone. Shak.
sterrink: The crab-eating seal (Lobodon carcinophaga) of the Antarctic Ocean.
stallman: One who keeps a stall for the sale of merchandise, especially books. Sterne.
stupa: A mound or monument commemorative of Buddha.
straight: A variant of Strait, a. [Obs. or R.] Egypt is a long country, but it is straight, that is to say, narrow. Sir J. Mandeville. | 1. Right, in a mathematical sense; passing from one point to another by the nearest course; direct; not deviating or crooked; as, a straight line or course; a straight piece of timber.
sterilization: The act or process of sterilizing, or rendering sterile; also, the state of being sterile.
stomp: To stamp with the foot. [Colloq.] "In gallant procession, the priests mean to stomp." R. Browning.
stupefier: One who, or that which, stupefies; a stupefying agent.
stipes: (a) The second joint of a maxilla of an insect or a crustacean. (b) An eyestalk.
stannic: Of or pertaining to tin; derived from or containing tin; specifically, designating those compounds in which the element has a higher valence as contrasted with stannous compounds. Stannic acid. (a) A hypothetical substance, Sn(OH)4, analogous to silic acid, and called also normal stannic acid. (b) Metastannic acid.
stableboy: A boy or man who attends in a stable; a groom; a hostler.
stockinet: An elastic textile fabric imitating knitting, of which stockings, under-garments, etc., are made.
strokesman: The man who rows the aftermost oar, and whose stroke is to be followed by the rest. Totten.
stager: 1. A player. B. Jonson. 2. One who has long acted on the stage of life; a practitioner; a person of experience, or of skill derived from long experience. "You will find most of the old stagers still stationary there." Sir W. Scott. 3. A horse used in drawing a stage. [Colloq.]
steeplechasing: The act of riding steeple chases.
steepy: Steep; precipitous. (poetic) No more, my goats, shall I belong you climb The steepy cliffs, or crop the flow'ry thyme. Dryden.
stonesmickle: The stonechat; -- called also stonesmitch. [Prov. Eng.]
stabling: 1. The act or practice of keeping horses and cattle in a stable. 2. A building, shed, or room for horses and cattle.
stricture: 1. Strictness. (old) A man of stricture and firm abstinence. Shak. 2. A stroke; a glance; a touch. (old) Sir M. Hale. 3. A touch of adverse criticism; censure. [I have] given myself the liberty of these strictures by way of reflection on all and every passage. Hammond. 4. (Med.) A localized morbid contraction of any passage of the body. Cf.
stoner: 1. One who stones; one who makes an assault with stones. 2. One who walls with stones.
stringed: 1. Having strings; as, a stringed instrument. Ps. cl. 4. 2. Produced by strings. "Answering the stringed noise." Milton.
stadtholdership: The office or position of a stadtholder.
statue: 1. The likeness of a living being sculptured or modeled in some solid substance, as marble, bronze, or wax; an image; as, a statue of Hercules, or of a lion. I will raise her statue in pure gold. | To place, as a statue; to form a statue of; to make into a statue. "The whole man becomes as if statued into stone and earth." Feltham.
steady: 1. Firm in standing or position; not tottering or shaking; fixed; firm. "The softest, steadiest plume." Keble. Their feet steady, their hands diligent, their eyes watchful, and their hearts resolute. | To make steady; to hold or keep from shaking, reeling, or falling; to make or keep firm; to support; to make constant, regular, or resolute.
strewing: 1. The act of scattering or spreading. 2. Anything that is, or may be, strewed; -- used chiefly in the plural. Shak.
stole: 1. A long, loose garment reaching to the feet. Spenser. But when mild morn, in saffron stole, First issues from her eastern goal. T. Warton. 2. (Eccl.) A narrow band of silk or stuff, sometimes enriched with embroidery and jewels, worn on the left shoulder of deacons, and across both shoulders of bishops and priests, pendent on each side nearly to the ground.
stibiated: Combined or impregnated with antimony (stibium). Stibiated tartar. See Tartar emetic, under Tartar.
stamina: 1. The fixed, firm part of a body, which supports it or gives it strength and solidity; as, the bones are the stamina of animal bodies; the ligneous parts of trees are the stamina which constitute their strength. 2. Whatever constitutes the principal strength or support of anything; power of endurance; backbone; vigor; as, the stamina of a constitution or of life;
stentorin: A blue coloring matter found in some stentors. See Stentor, 2.
strapshaped: Shaped like a strap; ligulate; as, a strap-shaped corolla.
stableness: The quality or state of being stable, or firmly established; stability.
staging: A structure of posts and boards for supporting workmen, etc., as in building. 2. The business of running stagecoaches; also, the act of journeying in stagecoaches.
storybook: A book containing stories, or short narratives, either true or false.
stumblingblock: Any cause of stumbling, perplexity, or error. We preach Christ crucified, unto the Jews a stumbling-block, and unto the Greeks foolishness. 1 Cor. i. 23.
stubborn: Firm as a stub or stump; stiff; unbending; unyielding; persistent; hence, unreasonably obstinate in will or opinion; not yielding to reason or persuasion; refractory; harsh; -- said of persons and things; as, stubborn wills; stubborn ore; a stubborn oak; as stubborn as a mule. "Bow, stubborn knees." Shak. "Stubborn attention and more than common application." Locke.
steam: 1. The elastic, aëriform fluid into which water is converted when heated to the boiling points; water in the state of vapor. 2. The mist formed by condensed vapor; visible vapor; | 1. To emit steam or vapor. My brother's ghost hangs hovering there, O'er his warm blood, that steams into the air. Dryden. Let the crude humors dance In heated brass, steaming with fire intence. J.
stupefaction: The act of stupefying, or the state of being stupefied. [Written also stupifaction.] Resistance of the dictates of conscience brings a hardness and stupefaction upon it. South.
steadiness: The quality or state of being steady. Steadiness is a point of prudence as well as of courage. L'Estrange. Syn. -- Constancy; resolution; unchangeableness.
stenographer: One who is skilled in stenography; a writer of shorthand.
studding: Material for studs, or joists; studs, or joists, collectively; studs.
styptic: Producing contraction; stopping bleeding; having the quality of restraining hemorrhage when applied to the bleeding part; astringent. [Written also stiptic.] Styptic weed (Bot.), an American leguminous herb (Cassia occidentalis) closely related to the wild senna.
stime: A slight gleam or glimmer; a glimpse. [Prov. Eng.] Halliwell.
stewardly: In a manner, or with the care, of a steward. To be stewardly dispensed, not wastefully spent. Tooker.
stammer: To make involuntary stops in uttering syllables or words; to hesitate or falter in speaking; to speak with stops and diffivulty; to stutter. I would thou couldst stammer, that thou mightest pour this… | To utter or pronounce with hesitation or imperfectly; -- sometimes with out.
stealthy: Done by stealth; accomplished clandestinely; unperceived; secret; furtive; sly. [Withered murder] with his stealthy pace, . . . Moves like a ghost. Shak.
stavewood: A tall tree (Simaruba amara) growing in tropical America. It is one of the trees which yields quassia.
staleness: The quality or state of being stale.
stylish: Having style or artistic quality; given to, or fond of, the display of style; highly fashionable; modish; as, a stylish dress, house, manner. -- Styl"ish*ly, adv. -- Styl"ish*ness, n.
stentor: 1. A herald, in the Iliad, who had a very loud voice; hence, any person having a powerful voice. 2. (Zoöl.) Any species of ciliated Infusoria belonging to the genus Stentor and allied genera, common in fresh water. The stentors have a bell-shaped, or cornucopia-like, body with a circle of cilia around the spiral terminal disk. See Illust. under Heterotricha. 3.
steeler: One who points, edges, or covers with steel.
starfish: 1. (Zoöl.) Any one of numerous species of echinoderms belonging to the class Asterioidea, in which the body is star-shaped and usually has five rays, though the number of rays varies from five to forty or more. stereobate: The lower part or basement of a building or pedestal; -- used loosely for several different forms of basement.
stogy: heavy; coarse; clumsy. [Colloq.] | 1. A stout, coarse boot or shoe; a brogan. 2. A kind of cheap, but not necessary inferior, cigar made in the form of a cylindrical roll.
standstill: A standing without moving forward or backward; a stop; a state or rest.
staphyloraphy: The operation of uniting a cleft palate, consisting in paring and bringing together the edges of the cleft. -- Staph`y*lo*raph"ic, Staph`y*lor*rhaph"ic, a.
stela: A small column or pillar, used as a monument, milestone, etc.
strived: Striven. Yea, so have I strived to preach the gospel. Rom. xv. 20.
strangeness: The state or quality of being strange (in any sense of the adjective).
stack: 1.
